23001.d: This is Willem Bosman’s 1703 account of his encounter with peoples & places of west Africa, whilst employed as Chief Factor (or Merchant) for the Dutch at the Castle of St George at Elmina (in modern day Ghana). The account gives fascinating historical information about the region. First written in dutch and translated into english (from 1705), this recording is based on the 1905 translation and offers extracts only - namely the author’s preface and six of his twenty-two letters i.e. letters -8,-9,-10,-18,-19 and -21. Please note: readers/listeners need to understand the context in which Bosman expresses his opinions & statements, influenced by the deep cultural biases of the eighteenth century ; chapter 21 refers to the Kingdom of Benin which sits within the modern state of Nigeria (not to be confused with the modern state of Bénin, formerly known as the Kingdom of Dahomey). To locate some of the areas referred to in this recording, readers may find the following public domain map useful: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:18th-century_maps_of_Nigeria#/media/File:Map_of_Slave_Coast-1789.jpg - Summary by Faith Abíọ́lá-Ellison

23004.d: Charles Eliot Norton (1827 – 1908) was an American author, social critic, and Harvard professor of art based in New England. He was considered by many of his contemporaries as the most cultivated man in America. Norton's prose translation of the Divine Comedy was published in 1891. His approach was that while it was not possible to reproduce the verse idiom of the original in another language, but that a translation could still capture the grandeur and richness of Dante's presentation. Previous translations in prose had been made by John Carlyle (brother of Thomas), W. S. Dugdale and A. J. Butler, and Norton acknowledges his debt to these. However, Norton felt that a new prose translation was warranted as the earlier prose versions were at times somewhat too literal. Speaking of his own translation, Norton writes in the introduction: "I have tried to be as literal in my translation as was consistent with good English, and to render Dante’s own words in words as nearly correspondent to them as the difference in the languages would permit." - Summary by Algy Pug

23008.d: LibriVox volunteers bring you 17 recordings of A Spot by Thomas hardy. This was the Weekly Poetry project for October 18, 2026. ------ Thomas Hardy was an English novelist, poet and architect. While Hardy wrote poetry throughout his life and regarded himself primarily as a poet, his first collection was not published until 1898. Initially, he gained fame as the author of novels such as Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), The Return of the Native (1878), The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891) and Jude the Obscure (1895). During his lifetime, Hardy's poetry was acclaimed by younger poets (particularly the Georgians) who viewed him as a mentor. - Summary by Wikipedia

23009.d: This volume contains English translations of two French mystery novels and two anonymous novelettes. The two novels, Count Kostia, by Victor Chebuliez (originally published in French in 1863) and Andre Cornelis, by Paul Bourget (1886) were made into films. Both of the novelettes are anonymous: The Last of the Costellos, and Lady Betty's Indiscretion. - Summary by Lynette Caulkins

23010.d: Alan Villiers and his friend, Ronald Walker, sign aboard the ship Grace Harwar to record the voyage around Cape Horn of one of the last great sailing ships. The voyage is filled with excitement, adventure, hard work, danger, and...death. Before setting sail aboard the Grace Harwar , Villiers was warned against doing so as the ship was known as a killer of men. Sadly, this warning comes true. - Summary by Barry Eads

23011.d: “Without these [letters,] one may learn much of his great achievements, such was his impress on his time and its records, but one does not know St. Basil. The letters soften that impression of hard-ness which the bare recital of strenuous exploit gives. They alone bring out in all its fullness that compound sternness and humour, kindliness and firmness that makes him one of the most attractive as he was one of the greatest of the Fathers.” (Summary from the Introduction)

23012.d: Six high school friends form a group called The Adventure Girls. Their first summer expedition to one of the girl’s family farms in Arizona find them deep into a mystery that needs solving. Follow them on their daily excursions and deadly encounters over the summer. A great read for young women and adults who enjoy young adult stories.

23013.d: This little work consists of a translation of the principal passages of the great treatise of Irenaeus against the heresies. It is not suggested that what has not been translated is of little value. A summary of such portions is supplied. But it is hoped that this will serve the student and average reader as an introduction to the deeper study of this great Church classic. Notes have been given wherever they were thought necessary, and the chain of the argument is shown throughout in order to facilitate the understanding of the work as a whole. - Summary by Preface

23014.d: With Christmas Day soon to arrive, Mr. Blake, pastor of the local church, is acutely aware of the needs of the poorer members of his congregation. But what can be done? The needs are many and deep. A dinner table conversation with his wife and children sparks a desire in their son, Willie, to try to make a difference in the lives of those less fortunate than himself. While Willie receives cooperation and encouragement from many in the community, it is the advice and urging of Old Hickory, his father's walking stick, which makes all the difference. NOTE: As with all historical texts, the language used in this volume should be interpreted within the context of the entire work and the cultural context of its publication. (Summary by Narrator)

23029.d: The republication of the theological works of Dr. Donne appeared to me highly desirable on my first reading the eighty sermons in 1831. On the appearance of Mr. Coleridge's Table Talk, in which he expresses very strongly his wish to the same effect, my desire was ripened into a plan of editing a selection from the sermons. I was fully sensible of my inadequacy, especially in antiquarian learning, to the task of giving a complete edition of Donne, as old authors are now edited: but I was willing to have enlarged opportunities of studying what appeared to me to be one of the earliest and best expositions of the divinity of our English church; and desirous that my first literary labour should be one likely to confer a benefit upon that Church, and upon English literature in general. - Summary by Editor
